notes:
These notes cover John 21:1–18 well, but verses 19–25 are thin. My search and fetch tools hit their usage limit partway through. I never got the Gill, Pulpit Commentary, Preceptaustin, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey or Orthodox (oca.org) pages. Lutheran, Wesleyan, Pentecostal and prosperity/word-of-faith views are also missing. Everything below comes from pages I actually read. Where only part of a page loaded, I say so.

---

**v. 1**
- "After these things" means some time had passed, not the next event. It links this chapter to the Gospel's first ending in 20:30–31. Ellicott says the Greek word for "showed himself" (manifested) does not support the claim that this chapter wasn't part of John's original Gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- This appearance happened in Galilee, as Matthew 28:16 also records. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- *Catholic (Augustine):* Augustine notes that 20:30–31 reads like the end of the book. He says the fishing scene that follows points to "the mystery of the Church" as it will be at the final resurrection. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott thinks the five named men are all the apostles in the group. The two unnamed ones were probably disciples in a wider sense. He finds it hard to believe they were Andrew and Philip. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik notes that Peter heads the list again. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan, who sees the two unnamed disciples as standing for the many faithful believers whose names are never recorded. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- *Augustine:* The seven disciples point to the end of time, because all time turns in cycles of seven days. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm

**v. 3**
- **Was Peter wrong to go fishing? Commentators disagree.**
  - Guzik lays out both views. Some say it was a compromised return to his old job; others say it was simply practical. Only Peter's heart could decide it. He points out that Jesus had told them to go to Galilee (Matthew 28:7, 10). He quotes Adam Clarke: they may have needed to earn a living now that their support from friends had dried up. He also quotes Leon Morris, who says the trip shows the disciples were unsure what to do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
  - Ellicott says the words show neither that they gave up their calling nor that they expected Jesus to appear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
  - Augustine raises the same question. He answers that the apostles were allowed, but not required, to live from the gospel rather than earn their own living. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm
- A night of catching nothing: Guzik quotes Spurgeon, who says Christ's ministers must expect disappointment and keep working in faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott says Jesus appeared suddenly, as in 20:19 and 26, and compares the disciples' failure to recognise him with Mary's in 20:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik suggests they may not have known him because they were caught up in their failure, or because of morning mist (quoting Tenney). He adds that Jesus came to them at their work, not only in worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- *Augustine:* The shore is the edge of the sea, so it stands for the end of the world. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm

**v. 5**
- "Children" was a common way to address working men, rather like "lads." It is not the tender word Jesus used in 13:33. To the disciples he would have sounded like a passing traveller. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 6**
- Ellicott thinks the disciples obeyed because the stranger on shore might have seen signs of fish on the other side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik quotes Plummer: don't look for hidden meaning in "right side." The real contrast is between working with God's guidance and without it. He also quotes F.F. Bruce, who sees the catch as a picture of the disciples' future mission, and recalls the similar catch in Luke 5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- *Augustine:* The Luke 5 catch pictures the Church now, with good and bad mixed together. This catch pictures the Church at the end, with only the good. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: John, the thinker, is first to recognise the Lord; Peter, the man of action, is first to rush to him. The garment Peter put on was a workman's outer frock. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik: John was first to recognise, but Peter was first in devotion. Quoting Morris and Dods, he explains that Peter was "naked" only in the sense of stripped down for work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 8**
- 200 cubits is about 100 yards. Being that close explains how they could tow the net in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott links the "fire of coals" to the fire in 18:18, where Peter denied Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik: Even after rising from the dead, Jesus is still a servant who cooks breakfast for them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 10**
- Jesus had food ready before the catch came in. What they caught added to the meal; it didn't make it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm

**v. 11 (the 153 fish)**
- **Traditional, plain reading:** Ellicott says the size and number are mentioned because fishermen would count an unusual catch and talk about it. He sees no intended hidden meaning and calls the symbolic readings "eccentricities of exegesis." He does accept the contrast with Luke 5, though: there the net broke, here no one is lost. The unbroken net is an eyewitness detail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm
- Guzik lists the old symbolic readings (Augustine, Jerome, Cyril, number-value theories). He concludes that we only know for certain it was the number of fish, and warns against inventing hidden meanings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- *Augustine:* 10 (the Law) plus 7 (the sevenfold Spirit) makes 17. Adding every number from 1 to 17 gives 153. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701122.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: The disciples felt they should ask who he was but couldn't bring themselves to, because they knew (quoting Bruce and Dods). He quotes Boice's list of Jesus' "come" invitations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 13**
- Guzik: A picture of close fellowship. Quoting Spurgeon, he imagines Peter looking at the fire with tears, remembering his denial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 14**
- "Third time" probably means the third appearance that John himself records (quoting Tasker). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 15**
- **"More than these" has two readings:**
  - More than the other disciples love me. This recalls Peter's boast in Matthew 26:33. Guzik prefers this view, and Barclay holds it too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/21-15.html
  - More than your old job of fishing. The bible.org Exegetical Commentary takes this view. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-21
- Jesus called him "Simon," not "Peter." Guzik suggests this may be a quiet reminder that he hadn't stood firm like a rock. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- **The two Greek words for love (agapaō and phileō):**
  - A real difference: Jesus first asks with *agapaō* (total, self-giving love) and Peter answers with *phileō* (friendship love). On this view Jesus is stretching Peter toward the higher love (GotQuestions), or Peter is being humbly careful after his failure (Guzik, most commentators). https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-Peter-do-you-love-me.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
  - No real difference: Constable notes that John uses both words for the Father's love for the Son and Jesus' love for Lazarus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/21-15.html
  - Reversed: one older comment on the same page takes *agapaō* as the weaker word and *phileō* as the stronger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/21-15.html
- **Protestant vs. Catholic: what was Peter restored to?**
  - *Reformed (Calvin):* Peter's denial had made him unworthy to be an apostle. Jesus' three-fold commission cancels the three denials, as Chrysostom and Augustine also said. It does not put Peter above the others. Christ entrusts only "his sheep" to pastors, and only the elect will benefit. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom35/calcom35.xi.ii.html ; https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_john_volume_2/john_21_15-19.htm
  - Ligonier: The three questions match the three denials and restore Peter to ministry. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-restores-peter
  - Another studylight commentary: Jesus says "my sheep," not "your sheep," which it reads as refuting the Pope's claims. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/awp/john-21.html
  - *Catholic:* "Feeding" and "tending" mean governing and teaching. Peter alone is given the whole flock, lambs and sheep, and his successors the bishops of Rome inherit this. Catholic writers grant that the scene makes up for the denials. But since all the apostles abandoned Jesus, they argue, singling out Peter must mean a unique leadership role. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-attempt-to-whitewash-peters-primacy ; https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/protestant-comebacks-when-catholics-say-peter-is-pope ; https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/where-does-the-bible-say-anything-about-the-papacy

**v. 16**
- The word for "feed" in vv. 15 and 17 means supplying food. "Tend" or "shepherd" here covers all of a shepherd's work, including guiding and rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/21-16.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- Clarke (quoted by Guzik) says this charge also applies to all later ministers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/

**v. 17**
- Peter was grieved because the third question clearly recalled his three denials. "You know all things" shows him trusting Jesus' knowledge of his heart rather than his own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-21/
- Bible.org: Three denials, three statements of love and three commissions leave no doubt that Peter was fully restored to apostolic leadership. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-21

**v. 18**
- **Was Jesus predicting crucifixion?**
  - Yes: "Stretch out your hands" was a common way of referring to crucifixion. Tradition says Peter was crucified (upside down) under Nero. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-predicts-peters-martyrdom ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/21-18.html
  - Clarke cites a Roman custom: the condemned had their arms stretched and tied to a yoke, then were led out to be crucified. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/21-18.html
  - Ellicott disagrees. He notes the tradition goes back to Tertullian but thinks the order of the words doesn't fit crucifixion. He reads the stretched hands as a sign of surrender, with the exact kind of death left open. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/21-18.htm

**v. 19**
- The man who was so afraid of arrest that he denied Christ would later follow him to the cross. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-predicts-peters-martyrdom

**v. 21**
- Coffman: Peter likely understood the grim meaning of Jesus' words, and natural curiosity prompted his question about John. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/john-21.html

**v. 24**
- Ellicott's outline treats this verse as a confirming witness to the Gospel from fellow disciples. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm

**v. 25**
- Ellicott's outline treats this verse as a confirming witness from the person who wrote down John's words (a secretary). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/21.htm

---

**Missing:** I have nothing usable on vv. 20, 22 and 23. That includes the rumour that John wouldn't die. Modern-scholarship views (such as whether chapter 21 was added later, and who the "we" in v. 24 is) and Orthodox readings are also missing. To finish these verses, the pages to read are the Gill and Pulpit Commentary verse pages on biblehub, netbible.org's John 21 notes, and Augustine's Tractates 123–124 on newadvent.org.
